description:
Chinook, a draughts program from the University of Alberta, finished second to Marion Tinsley at the 1990 US Nationals. All of its knowledge was programmed by its creators rather than learned.

The governing bodies refused to let a computer play for the world title, so Tinsley resigned his title in protest and played the match anyway. He won in 1992 with four wins to Chinook's two, and 33 draws.

the total number of games Tinsley lost from 1950 until his death in 1995. Two of them were to Chinook.

In their 1994 rematch, all six games were drawn. Then Tinsley withdrew, ill with pancreatic cancer, and Chinook was declared champion. He died the following April.

In 2007 the same team proved that draughts, played perfectly by both sides, always ends in a draw. Published in Science as 'Checkers Is Solved'.

Sources:
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinook_(computer_program): confirms Chinook was built at the University of Alberta by a team led by Jonathan Schaeffer; that all its knowledge was programmed by hand rather than learned; that it qualified for the World Championship by finishing second to Marion Tinsley at the 1990 US Nationals; that the governing bodies refused a computer entry until Tinsley resigned his title in protest; that Tinsley won their match with four wins to Chinook's two and 33 draws; that in 1994 Chinook became Man-Machine World Champion after six drawn games and Tinsley's withdrawal due to pancreatic cancer, without ever defeating him; and that the team's paper 'Checkers Is Solved' was published in Science on 19 July 2007, proving perfect play ends in a draw.
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marion_Tinsley: confirms Tinsley lost only seven games from 1950 until his death in 1995, two of them to Chinook; that the unofficial match was played in August 1992; that he was diagnosed with pancreatic cancer a week after the 1994 match; and that he died on 3 April 1995.
